title: Information Is Becoming Cheap. Decision-Making Is Becoming Invaluable.
summary: Sales data updates in real time. Labor performance can be monitored across locations. Guest feedback is constantly collected. Inventory, loyalty, digital ordering and operational metrics generate a steady stream of information.
body_markdown:
## Direct Answer


Restaurant operators have more information than ever before.


Sales data updates in real time. Labor performance can be monitored across locations. Guest feedback is constantly collected. Inventory, loyalty, digital ordering and operational metrics generate a steady stream of information. Now AI is making it possible to surface even more insights, recommendations and opportunities in a matter of seconds.


Yet despite all that visibility, many operators are still asking a difficult question: **What deserves my attention right now?**


‍


### Key Takeaways


- Visibility has improved dramatically across the restaurant industry.
- AI is increasing the volume of available insights and recommendations.
- More information does not automatically create better outcomes.
- Leadership increasingly depends on prioritization and trade-off decisions.
- High-performing operators focus on outcomes rather than metrics alone.
- The next evolution of restaurant technology is helping organizations act with confidence.


‍


The challenge facing restaurant leaders is no longer access to information. It's determining which signals matter, which actions will create the greatest impact and where finite time and resources should be invested.


As information becomes easier to collect, analyze and distribute, decision-making is becoming one of the most valuable capabilities in restaurant operations. The organizations that outperform their peers won't necessarily be the ones with more data. They'll be the ones that consistently turn information into action.


‍


## Restaurant Leaders Don’t Have an Information Problem


Talk to enough restaurant operators today and a common pattern begins to emerge.


Very few are asking for another dashboard. They're not struggling to find data. In many cases, they're overwhelmed by it.


A multi-location restaurant brand may simultaneously be monitoring labor costs, menu performance, loyalty engagement, guest feedback, inventory trends, third-party delivery activity and dozens of other operational indicators. Layer AI-generated recommendations on top of that, and the volume of information increases even further.


Imagine sitting down on Monday morning and discovering:


- Labor costs are trending above target in several markets.
- Loyalty engagement has slipped for a key customer segment.
- A high-margin menu item is underperforming expectations.
- Guest sentiment has declined at a handful of locations.
- An AI tool has identified five additional opportunities to improve performance.


None of those insights are inherently wrong. Each one may deserve attention. The task becomes figuring out where to start.


For years, the restaurant industry focused on improving visibility. Today, many operators are experiencing the unintended consequence of that success: they have access to more information than they can realistically act on.


That's a very different problem than the one the industry was trying to solve a decade ago.


‍


## The Industry Got What It Asked For


The industry responded aggressively. Reporting tools became more sophisticated. Dashboards became more accessible. Data that once required days of analysis became available almost instantly. Leaders could review labor performance, menu trends, inventory movement, guest satisfaction and sales metrics from virtually anywhere.


At NCR Voyix, we've spent years helping restaurant operators increase visibility across their businesses, giving us a firsthand view of how access to information has evolved from a competitive advantage into an operational expectation.


What's become more evident is that the next challenge isn't generating more information. It's helping operators understand what deserves action


The conversations we're having with customers today sound very different than they did five or ten years ago. Operators aren't asking whether they can access data. They're asking how to prioritize it.


‍


## When More Information Creates More Questions


A labor exception report might identify a problem. Guest feedback might reveal dissatisfaction with a product. Sales data might uncover an opportunity\[EJ2.1\]. Restaurants today find themselves in a situation where not all opportunities deserve the same level of attention because not all actions deliver the same business impact. Yet with so much information readily available, none of these insights automatically answer the most important question: What should happen next? The real challenge is determining which action will create the greatest value for the business.


Many operators start their day with a steady flow of metrics, alerts, reports and recommendations. Some will point to short-term issues. Others suggest long-term opportunities. Still others highlight anomalies that may not require action at all. The challenge is rarely a lack of visibility. It is deciding where to focus finite time, money and operational energy.


Restaurant executives are not rewarded because they review more dashboards than their competitors. They are rewarded because they allocate resources effectively and make sound choices under pressure. Technology can provide context, but judgment determines outcomes.


This is where the conversation around AI becomes especially interesting.


‍


## The Conversation Around AI Misses Something Important


Much of the public discussion focuses on AI's ability to surface insights. It can identify patterns within large data sets, summarize information and uncover trends that might otherwise be overlooked. Those capabilities are valuable. They also represent a dramatic shift in the economics of information.


Historically, insights were expensive. Generating them required analysis, specialized expertise and significant effort. Today, many of those steps can be compressed into seconds. As AI capabilities advance, organizations will have access to more observations, recommendations and predictions than ever before.


The challenge is that AI is only as effective as the information and systems supporting it. As restaurant technology evolves toward cloud-native and microservices-based architectures, operators gain greater flexibility to introduce new capabilities, connect new data sources and adapt as business needs change. That sounds entirely positive until you recognize that an abundance of recommendations can create a different kind of complexity.


That's why the conversation around AI can't be separated from platforms. Modern, cloud-native architectures built around microservices make it easier to connect operational data across the business, giving operators a more complete foundation for decision-making.


As operators introduce new technologies, ordering channels and data sources, information must be connected before it can become actionable. Otherwise, AI risks generating recommendations based on only part of the picture.


At NCR Voyix, we hear how operators are actively trying to clean up their disconnected insights. They're looking for a clearer understanding of what's happening across the business and how to respond. The more information flows through a common platform, the easier it becomes to evaluate competing priorities, identify meaningful opportunities and act with confidence.


That's important because an abundance of recommendations can create a different kind of complexity. When information becomes easier to generate, the competitive advantage doesn't come from producing more insights. It comes from understanding which insights deserve action.


‍


## Information Used to Be the Product


Operators invested in reporting because information was difficult to obtain. Dashboards created value because visibility was limited. Analysts created value because interpreting large volumes of data required specialized expertise. In many ways, information itself was the product.


If you could uncover a trend before a competitor, identify a problem sooner or gain a clearer view of operational performance, you had an advantage. That's what made reporting and analytics so valuable for so long. Today, that equation is changing.


AI can summarize reports in seconds. It can identify anomalies, uncover patterns and generate recommendations faster than most teams could manually analyze a single spreadsheet.


In other words, the cost of generating information is steadily declining. That's an extraordinary advancement for the industry. But it also changes where value is created.


When information becomes easier to produce, information itself becomes less differentiated. The competitive advantage shifts.


‍


> ‍ *Two operators may have access to the same data, the same dashboards and even the same AI-generated recommendations. Yet one organization may outperform the other because it makes better decisions about where to focus its people, resources and capital.*


‍


That's why I believe decision-making is becoming more valuable than information itself.


‍


## Interesting Is Not Always Important


Imagine a system highlighting staffing inefficiencies, menu opportunities, inventory concerns, guest experience trends and forecast adjustments simultaneously. Every recommendation may be reasonable. Every recommendation may be supported by data. Yet the organization still must decide which one deserves attention first.


The real question is whether leaders can determine which opportunities will create the greatest business impact.


That distinction moves the discussion beyond analytics and into decision-making.


One of the most overlooked challenges in modern business is the ability to separate information that is interesting from information that is consequential. Those categories are not synonymous.


Organizations encounter fascinating data every day. A customer segment behaves differently than expected. A menu item performs unusually well in one market. A location deviates from established benchmarks. These findings may be worth understanding, but they do not always justify action.


The strongest operators evaluate information through the lens of outcomes. They ask whether a finding influences profitability, efficiency, guest experience or strategic objectives. They connect observations to business priorities rather than treating every metric as equally significant.


‍


## The Best Operators Focus on Outcomes


In many organizations, the temptation is to treat more visibility as inherently beneficial. Yet there is a point where additional information delivers diminishing returns unless it contributes to a better decision. The goal is not comprehensive awareness of every operational detail. The goal is improving performance.


Instead of asking what additional reports can be generated, they ask which decisions are most important. Instead of evaluating dashboards in isolation, they consider how information supports larger business objectives. Instead of measuring success by the quantity of available insights, they evaluate whether those insights create meaningful outcomes.


The difference may seem subtle, but it is significant. One approach treats information as the destination. The other treats information as an input.


The highest-performing restaurant operators rarely chase every signal. They establish priorities, understand the operational drivers that matter most and remain disciplined about where they focus attention. Doing so enables them to avoid being distracted by activity that creates little value.


This ability to prioritize is becoming more important precisely because information is becoming easier to obtain.


We have seen similar patterns emerge in other industries. When access to something expands dramatically, the advantage gained from mere possession often declines. The differentiator moves elsewhere.


Execution produces results. Judgment produces results. The ability to weigh competing priorities and choose a course of action produces results.


That is why leadership remains such a critical component of operational success regardless of how sophisticated technology becomes.


‍


## The Next Challenge for Restaurant Technology


At NCR Voyix, we believe the next evolution of restaurant technology isn't simply helping operators see more. It's helping them focus on what matters most.


Visibility will always be the standard. Data will always be important. AI will continue making insights more accessible than ever before.


But information alone doesn't improve restaurant performance. Decisions do.


That's why we see that the future of restaurant technology isn’t being defined by the volume of information systems can generate. The ability to help operators confidently translate that information into action will be much more important.


Because as information becomes cheaper, the value of good judgment only increases.


‍


#### Frequently asked questions


**Why are restaurant operators focusing so heavily on data?**
Because operations have become more complex and visibility helps leaders understand performance across locations, channels and workflows.


**Has the industry solved the visibility challenge?**
Visibility has improved substantially, but the challenge is now translating information into effective action.


**How does AI change decision-making? ‍** AI can surface opportunities faster, increasing the importance of prioritization and business context.


**What makes a piece of information valuable? ‍** Its ability to influence a meaningful business outcome, not simply its novelty.


**Why is prioritization becoming so important? ‍** Organizations have limited time and resources, making trade-off decisions essential.


**What separates high-performing operators? ‍** Clear priorities, disciplined execution and a focus on outcomes rather than metrics alone.


**What should restaurant technology do next? ‍** Help operators connect information to decisions and decisions to measurable business results.
